7972	Finally, the finite linear-forest polynomial satisfies
7973	\[
7974	\log p_F(z)=2e(F)z-2(e(F)+w(F))z^2+O_F(z^3).
7975	\]
7976	Equal finite edge counts cancel the linear term; putting \(z=(qn)^{-1}\) proves (4). ∎

7979	
7980	## 2. The structural reduction
7981	
7982	We use two classical results in their usual forms:
7983	
7984	* Erdős–Stone and Erdős–Simonovits stability;
7985	* Bregman’s permanent inequality.
7986	
7987	No exact Simonovits extremal classification is needed.
7988	
7989	A *star decomposition* means that \(H\) embeds in a complete \(r\)-partite graph with a fixed star added inside one part. A *linear-forest decomposition* is defined similarly.
7990	
7991	### Structural lemma
7992	
7993	Suppose \(H\) has chromatic number \(r+1\), a critical vertex, and a linear-forest decomposition.
7994	
7995	* Every sufficiently large edge extremizer has a partition into \(r\) parts of sizes \(n/r+o(n)\), bounded internal components, and only boundedly many holes, all between a bounded set of exceptional components.
7996	* For \(r\ge3\), the same holds for cycle extremizers.
7997	
7998	Here is the proof, including the cycle-regularization step.
7999	
8000	### 2.1. Stability and a regular core
8001	
8002	For a cycle extremizer \(G\),
8003	\[
8004	2c(G)+1\le \operatorname{per}(I+A_G).
8005	\]
8006	Bregman, Stirling, and arithmetic–geometric mean give
8007	\[
8008	\operatorname{per}(I+A_G)
8009	 \le \left(\frac{2e(G)/n+O(\log n)}e\right)^n.
8010	\]
8011	The counting lemma gives
8012	\(c(T_{n,r})=n!q^n\exp(o(n))\). Hence
8013	\(e(G)\ge t_r(n)-o(n^2)\), so stability applies. For edge extremizers stability applies directly.
8014	
8015	There is thus a regular core, missing at most \(\varepsilon n\) opposite-part neighbors per core vertex, and an exceptional set \(X_0\) of size \(o(n)\).
8016	
8017	A critical vertex supplies a star decomposition, say with \(\mu\) leaves. A greedy embedding shows:
8018	
8019	* no vertex has at least \(\eta n\) core neighbors in every part;
8020	* if exactly one part is \(\eta\)-sparse for a vertex, it has fewer than \(\mu\) core neighbors in that part.
8021	
8022	Assign each exceptional vertex to a sparse part. A vertex sparse to two parts has at most \(\eta n\) assigned-part core neighbors; one with a unique sparse part has \(O_H(1)\).
8023	
8024	Call a vertex truly bad if it misses at least \(\delta n\) vertices in an opposite core part, where
8025	\[
8026	\varepsilon\ll\eta\ll\delta\ll |H|^{-1}.
8027	\]
8028	
8029	Replacing all truly bad vertices by pure vertices of their assigned parts is \(H\)-safe. Indeed, in any new copy of \(H\), remap the newly pure vertices greedily to old core vertices in the corresponding parts. Every fixed image excludes at most \(\delta n+o(n)\) candidates, leaving a positive common neighborhood.
8030	
8031	For edge extremizers this operation gains \(\Omega(n)\) crossedges per replaced vertex and loses only \(O_H(1)+o(n)\), or at most \(\eta n+o(n)\), internal edges. Thus no truly bad vertex exists.
8032	
8033	### 2.2. Why the replacement also increases cycles when \(r\ge3\)
8034	
8035	We give the switching count explicitly.
8036	
8037	For an oriented path
8038	\[
8039	u=p_0,\ldots,p_i=w,\ldots,p_j=z,\ldots,p_{\ell-1}=v,
8040	\]
8041	rotate first at \(z\), then at \(w\), keeping endpoint \(v\). The added edges are
8042	\[
8043	up_{j+1},\quad
8044	\begin{cases}
8045	zp_{i-1},&j>i,\\
8046	zp_{i+1},&j<i.
8047	\end{cases}                                                 \tag{8}
8048	\]
8049	For regular endpoints and target neighbors, there are \(\Omega_r(n)\) valid pivots. Indeed, on any path segment with \(L\) vertices, \(h\) vertices in one part, and \(b\) same-part steps,
8050	\[
8051	2h\le L+b+1.
8052	\]
8053	Thus on a near-spanning path with \(o(n)\) same-part steps the exclusions in (8) total at most
8054	\[
8055	\frac nr+\frac n2+o(n)<n.
8056	\]
8057	This is where \(r\ge3\) is essential.
8058	
8059	Before replacement, add \(\zeta n\) regular neighbors in each opposite part to every truly bad vertex, choosing
8060	\(\eta\ll\zeta\ll\delta\). These edges all survive its eventual purification. An arbitrary endpoint can then first be made regular by one rotation, in \(\Omega(\zeta n)\) ways.
8061	
8062	Let a bad vertex \(x\) have \(s\) internal neighbors and \(d\) missing crossneighbors. Delete \(x\) from a cycle. Transferring a specified old endpoint to one of the missing neighbors has
8063	\(\Omega(dn^2)\) forward descriptions; if the old endpoint lies in a set of size \(s\), there are only \(O(sn^2)\) inverse descriptions. Repairing both ends gives the square of this ratio.
8064	
8065	Consequently, cycles using one or two deleted internal edges yield respectively at least
8066	\[
8067	c\,\frac ds,\qquad c\left(\frac ds\right)^2
8068	\]
8069	times as many gained cycles. Retained cycles containing \(x\) also yield at least \(cd/n\) gained cycles per old cycle. Here \(s=o(n)\) in the unique-sparse case, and \(s\le\eta n+o(n)\) in the two-sparse case, so the gain exceeds the loss.
8070	
8071	Cycles omitting \(x\) cause no problem: each near-spanning such cycle has \(\Omega(n)\) edges outside the assigned part, into which the new pure \(x\) can be inserted.
8072	
8073	The omitted short cycles and cycles with linearly many internal steps are negligible. Their counts are at most
8074	\[
8075	n^{(1-\gamma)n+O(1)}
8076	\quad\text{or}\quad
8077	n^n2^n(Q_0/n)^{\tau n/2-O(1)},
8078	\]
8079	because regular-core internal degree \(Q_0\) is bounded. Both are
8080	\(\exp(-\Omega(n\log n))\) below the factorial cycle scale.
8081	
8082	Successively purifying all truly bad vertices therefore increases cycles. Only the final graph needs to be \(H\)-free, and its safety was proved above. Thus a cycle extremizer has no truly bad vertices.
8083	
8084	### 2.3. Bounded components and bounded holes
8085	
8086	All vertices are now cross-\(\delta n\)-regular. The star decomposition bounds global internal degree by \(\mu-1\). The linear-forest decomposition forbids a sufficiently long internal path. Bounded degree and bounded longest path imply bounded component order.
8087	
8088	For \(r\ge3\), the same two-rotation count gives:
8089	
8090	* a fixed vertex is omitted from \(O(c(G)/n)\) cycles;
8091	* a fixed internal edge lies in \(O(c(G)/n)\) cycles;
8092	* completing \(d\) holes at a vertex creates at least \(cd\,c(G)/n\) cycles.
8093	
8094	The third assertion remains valid for constant \(d\): average over targets, using the first assertion, rather than assuming every long cycle contains every target.
8095	
8096	Purify an entire bounded internal component. Completing its crossedges gains \(\Omega(d\,c(G)/n)\), while deleting its boundedly many internal edges loses \(O(c(G)/n)\). Hence maximum hole degree is bounded. The edge version is simpler: the edge gain is at least \(d-O_H(1)\).
8097	
8098	There are now finitely many component types, including their part labels. Call a type abundant if it has more than
8099	\[
8100	|H|(M_0+1)
8101	\]
8102	copies, where \(M_0\) bounds hole degree. All other components occupy boundedly many vertices.
8103	
8104	Fill every hole incident with an abundant component. This is \(H\)-safe: remap every selected abundant component of a purported new \(H\)-copy to an unused old copy. At most \(|H|\) copies are excluded by injectivity and at most \(|H|M_0\) by missing crossedges. A copy therefore remains available.
8105	
8106	Every added crossedge increases edges, and, for \(r\ge3\), creates a triangle. Extremality says there were no such holes. This proves the structural lemma. ∎
8107	
8108	---
8109	
8110	## 3. Universal exclusion below the claimed thresholds
8111	
8112	Assume
8113	\[
8114	\operatorname{ex}(n,H)\le t_r(n)+an+O(1),\qquad a<1/r.        \tag{9}
8115	\]
8116	
8117	The graph \(K_1\vee T_{n-1,r}\) has
8118	\(t_r(n)+n/r+O(1)\) edges, so it contains \(H\). Thus \(H\) has a critical vertex.
8119	
8120	Likewise, adding a spanning path inside one part of \(T_{n,r}\) gives surplus \(n/r+O(1)\). It contains \(H\), so \(H\) has a linear-forest decomposition. The structural lemma applies.
8121	
8122	An abundant component is freely repeatable: a copy of \(H\) using arbitrarily many new copies could be remapped to old abundant copies. Therefore:
8123	
8124	* no abundant component is cyclic, since repeating it gives surplus at least \(n/r-O(1)\);
8125	* at most one part has nontrivial abundant components, since two tree-active parts each have density at least \(1/2\), again giving surplus at least \(n/r-O(1)\).
8126	
8127	Let \(k\) be the largest order of an admissible repeated tree. It is finite, by the degree and path bounds, and
8128	\[
8129	\frac{k-1}{kr}\le a.                                        \tag{10}
8130	\]
8131	Both edge and cycle extremizers must use order \(k\): smaller orders lose a linear number of edges or, by (1), a fixed positive factor in cycles.
8132	
8133	There are only boundedly many smaller components. Otherwise, among \(k\) such components, some nonempty subcollection has total order divisible by \(k\). Replacing it by full \(k\)-trees gains an edge. It is \(H\)-safe by abundance remapping, and increases cycles by
8134	\(1+2/(qn)+o(n^{-1})\), contradicting either extremality.
8135	
8136	All smaller components can thus be absorbed into a bounded context.
8137	
8138	### 3.1. Part sizes are boundedly imbalanced
8139	
8140	Keep the context and rebalance the parts, filling the active part with copies of an admissible \(k\)-tree and one subtree for the remainder. This is \(H\)-safe by the same remapping argument.
8141	
8142	Its internal edge count differs by \(O(1+\|\delta\|)\). Applying (1) and extremality gives
8143	\[
8144	Q\le C(1+\|\delta\|)+o(Q),
8145	\]
8146	so \(\|\delta\|=O_H(1)\). For edge extremizers the same conclusion follows directly from the quadratic crossedge loss.
8147	
8148	There are therefore finitely many phases. In each phase the maximal net internal contribution at active-part size \(a\) has the exact form
8149	\[
8150	m_u(a)=a-\left\lceil\frac{a-u}{k}\right\rceil+d,               \tag{11}
8151	\]
8152	where \(u,d\) are fixed integers. Holes and bounded context edges are included in \(d\).
8153	
8154	### 3.2. Exact phase optimization
8155	
8156	For \(k\)-vertex trees,
8157	\[
8158	k-2\le w(T)\le\binom{k-1}{2}.
8159	\]
8160	The path and star attain the two endpoints, giving the per-vertex gap
8161	\[
8162	D_k=\frac{(k-2)(k-3)}{2k}.                                  \tag{12}
8163	\]
8164	
8165	Put \(n=rm+s\), \(0\le s<r\). In an edge- or first-order-cycle-optimal phase, only active sizes \(m,m+1,m+2\) need be considered; \(m+2\) is possible only for \(s\ge2\).
8166	
8167	Indeed, increasing the active size by one, from a largest inactive part of size \(b\), changes the crossedge count by \(b-a-1\) and the internal count by \(0\) or \(1\). If \(a>b\), the cycle score decreases. If \(a\) is smaller than all other parts, increasing it improves both objectives.
8168	
8169	At the only potentially conflicting step the crossedge loss is one, and the extra part score is
8170	\[
8171	P=2L(2\rho-1).
8172	\]
8173	If the internal increment is one, the edge counts tie and the cycle score favors the larger active part. If it is zero, the cycle-score loss is

1	# An explicit Bregman near-extremal-edge reduction
2	
3	For every n>=2 put L=3(log(n+1)+1). For 1<=k<=n,
4	  (k!)^(1/k) <= (k+L)/e.
5	Indeed log(k!) <= k log k-k+log k+1 by integral comparison.
6	If k<=L/(e-1), then (k+L)/e>=k>=(k!)^(1/k).
7	Otherwise k log(1+L/k)>=Lk/(k+L)>L/e>log(n)+1>=log(k)+1.
8	
9	For adjacency matrix A of G, every unoriented simple cycle gives TWO
10	permutations contributing to per(A+I), all other vertices being fixed.
11	Therefore 2c(G)+1 <= per(A+I). Bregman's theorem and AM-GM imply
12	  2c(G)+1 <= product_v [(d(v)+1+L)/e]
13	            <= [(2e(G)/n+1+L)/e]^n.
14	This explicit version does not require a concavity assertion about factorial
15	roots or a minimum-degree assumption.
16	
17	For fixed r>=2, the standard exact multipartite color-word count (or its
18	local central limit estimate) gives
19	  c(T_{n,r}) >= n! ((r-1)/r)^n / n^K
20	for some fixed K=K(r), along the appropriate parity classes for r=2.
21	Consequently if c(G)>=c(T_{n,r}), the displayed Bregman bound gives
22	  e(G)>=t_r(n)-O_r(n log n).
23	Combining with Erdos-Simonovits stability, for H-free G with chi(H)=r+1,
24	any cycle extremizer is o(n^2)-close to a balanced complete r-partite graph.
25	
26	This only proves the initial approximate-structure reduction; it does not
27	assert the exact bounded-template result needed later.
